lesson.title: Counting What Actually Happened
lesson.summary: Observed counts are the raw tallies you actually collect in a frequency table, and they are the raw material every chi-square test is built from.
lesson.body:
Every chi-square procedure starts in the same humble place: a count of what actually happened. An observed count is simply the number of individuals, trials, or outcomes in your data that fall into a particular category of a frequency table. If you survey 100 students about their favorite season and 22 of them say spring, then 22 is an observed count. It is not a percentage, not a proportion, not a guess about what should happen. It is a tally of what you actually saw.

Suppose a teacher surveys 100 students and builds this frequency table of favorite season: Spring 22, Summer 35, Fall 18, Winter 25. Check the arithmetic: 22 plus 35 plus 18 plus 25 equals 100, which matches the sample size, a good habit to build every time you read or build a frequency table. Each of those four numbers, 22, 35, 18, and 25, is an observed count. Together they describe the distribution of favorite season in this particular sample of 100 students.

Observed counts matter because every chi-square test that follows in this unit works by comparing them to a second set of numbers called expected counts, the counts you would predict if some claim about the population were true. The whole logic of a chi-square test is to measure how far the observed counts drift from the expected counts, then ask whether that drift is more than random sampling variation would explain. Without a solid, correctly tallied set of observed counts, that comparison cannot even get started.

One practical trap: reports often hand you percentages instead of raw counts. If a summary says 22% of a sampled group preferred spring out of a sample of 150, you cannot plug 22 directly into chi-square arithmetic. You first have to recover the count: 0.22 times 150 equals 33 people. Chi-square procedures need actual counts of people or things, not rates, because the arithmetic ahead, squaring differences and dividing by expected counts, only makes sense on counts. You will meet observed counts again in two different shapes: as a single row of categories from one sample, as above, and as the cells of a two-way table crossing two variables or several groups, which is where the goodness-of-fit, homogeneity, and independence tests of the rest of this unit all begin.
